title: Enterprise Risk Management — MBG's Risk Register (CMA P2-D · feeds AUD/ISC)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — MBG's real risks are not hypothetical

Real MBG facts: $400,000.00 sits stranded in 7 dormant accounts (liquidity risk), 15 expired certificates of insurance left $512,000.00 of exposure uncovered (compliance risk), Account 111 carries an unreconciled $95,000.00 (process risk), and the company depends heavily on surety bonding and a concentrated banking relationship. Enterprise risk management (ERM) is the discipline of identifying, assessing, responding to, and monitoring these risks across the whole entity rather than in silos.

ERM versus traditional risk management

Traditional risk management treats risks one at a time, usually as something to insure. ERM is enterprise-wide and strategy-linked: it considers how risks interact, ties risk to objectives, and weighs both downside and upside. The COSO ERM framework (2017) organizes this into five components — governance and culture; strategy and objective-setting; performance; review and revision; and information, communication, and reporting — supported by twenty principles.

Risk appetite and tolerance

Risk appetite is the broad amount of risk an entity is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives; risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around a specific objective. For MBG, a low appetite for liquidity and compliance risk should translate into concrete tolerances: a minimum working-capital floor that protects bonding capacity, and zero tolerance for an expired certificate of insurance on an active job. Appetite without measurable tolerances is just a slogan.

Inherent versus residual risk and the four-plus-one responses

Inherent risk is the exposure before any response; residual risk is what remains after controls. Management chooses a response for each significant risk: accept (within tolerance), avoid (exit the activity), reduce (controls that lower likelihood or impact), share/transfer (insurance, surety, indemnification), and — uniquely in ERM — pursue (take more of a risk that advances strategy). MBG's expired-COI exposure calls for reduce (a compliance-tracking control) and transfer (valid insurance), not acceptance.

Building MBG's risk register

A risk register lists each risk with its owner, inherent likelihood and impact, current controls, residual rating, and response. An illustrative MBG register: liquidity risk (dormant cash, thin usable balances) — owner CFO, response reduce via cash sweep; surety/bonding concentration — response reduce via working-capital build; compliance risk (COI gaps) — response reduce and transfer; single-bank concentration — response reduce via a second banking relationship; process risk (unreconciled clearing accounts) — response reduce via monthly reconciliation to $0. Governance and culture sit above all of it: the board sets the tone, and the transaction registry and segregation of duties make the controls real.

Structure, the three lines, and ERM versus internal control

Beneath the five components sit twenty principles that operationalize them — for example, the governance-and-culture component includes principles on board oversight, operating structures, and a commitment to integrity and ethical values. The exam rarely asks the list verbatim, but it does test the logic: each component is a set of principles an organization must demonstrate, and a gap in any one weakens the whole framework. ERM is also broader than internal control: internal control (the COSO 2013 framework, month five) is primarily about reliable reporting, compliance, and operational effectiveness, while ERM (COSO 2017) is explicitly tied to strategy and performance — it asks not only "are our controls working?" but "are we taking the right risks to achieve our objectives?"

Responsibility for risk is organized through the three lines model. The first line is operational management, which owns and manages risk directly — the project managers and superintendents who run MBG's jobs. The second line is risk, compliance, and finance functions that set policy, monitor, and challenge — the CFO and controller maintaining the risk register and the COI-compliance program. The third line is internal audit, which provides independent assurance to the board that the first two lines are working. Keeping the lines distinct is itself a control: the people who run the work should not be the only ones assessing whether its risks are managed.

Risk appetite into action

Risk appetite becomes useful only when translated into measurable tolerances and decision rules. For MBG, a low appetite for liquidity risk turns into a concrete working-capital floor that protects bonding capacity, a maximum share of revenue from any single customer, and a hard rule that no job starts without a current certificate of insurance on file. Each significant risk then receives a documented response — accept, avoid, reduce, share, or pursue — with an owner and a monitoring metric. A risk register that lists exposures without appetite-linked tolerances and assigned owners is a document, not a program; ERM is the discipline of closing that gap so the board's stated appetite actually shapes day-to-day decisions.

Common ERM pitfalls

Three traps recur: treating ERM as a compliance checklist divorced from strategy rather than a tool for choosing which risks to take; maintaining a static register that is updated annually instead of as conditions change; and a weak risk culture in which the tone at the top tolerates working around controls when a deadline is tight. The framework only works when culture, structure, and measurable tolerances reinforce one another.

Monitoring, assurance, and risk maturity

ERM is a continuous cycle, not a one-time setup: risks are monitored against their indicators, responses are tracked to completion, and the program is periodically reassessed as strategy and conditions change. Ongoing supervisory review plus separate evaluations confirm that responses operate, while internal audit — the third line — gives the board independent assurance that the framework is effective. A risk reduced to an acceptable residual level last year can drift back into the red if the control degrades or the exposure grows, which is exactly why monitoring closes the loop the register opens.

Organizations also differ in risk maturity. A low-maturity firm manages risk reactively and in silos; a high-maturity firm has embedded risk thinking into strategy, capital allocation, and incentives, with a common language and clear ownership. For MBG, maturing the program means moving from "the CFO keeps a spreadsheet of worries" to risk-informed decisions about which jobs to bond, how much working-capital cushion to hold, and how much backlog to concentrate in a single customer — the point where ERM stops being a document and starts shaping the business. The throughline of this month is that the same discipline applies whether the risk is liquidity, a lapsed certificate of insurance, or an unreconciled clearing account: identify it, rate it, assign an owner and a response, monitor it against a measurable tolerance, and let independent assurance confirm the controls are real.

CPA Crossover — AUD / ISC

AUD applies risk assessment to the audit (inherent and control risk, the risk of material misstatement); ISC applies it to IT and data risk. The COSO components, the inherent-versus-residual distinction, and the response taxonomy are shared vocabulary across CMA, AUD, and ISC.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish ERM (enterprise-wide, strategy-linked) from siloed risk management.
  2. Set risk appetite and translate it into measurable tolerances.
  3. Separate inherent from residual risk and choose accept/avoid/reduce/share/pursue.
  4. Build a risk register with owners, ratings, controls, and responses.

Recap: ERM manages MBG's real exposures — stranded cash, COI gaps, unreconciled clearing, bonding and bank concentration — as an interacting portfolio. Appetite becomes tolerances, inherent risk becomes residual through chosen responses, and governance makes it stick.

flashcards.back: ERM is enterprise-wide and strategy-linked, considering interacting risks and upside; traditional handles risks in silos, mostly via insurance.
Governance & culture; strategy & objective-setting; performance; review & revision; information, communication & reporting.

Inherent = exposure before response; residual = what remains after controls.
Accept, avoid, reduce, share/transfer, and pursue.

flashcards.front: Appropriate response to MBG's expired-COI exposure
flashcards.back: Reduce (compliance tracking control) and transfer (valid insurance), not accept.

flashcards.front: Where does governance sit in ERM?
flashcards.back: Above the controls — the board sets the tone and culture that make controls effective.

questions.q: How does ERM differ from traditional risk management?
choices: It is enterprise-wide and strategy-linked, considering interacting risks
It handles one risk at a time
questions.explain: ERM manages risk across the entity and links it to strategy, considering both downside and upside.

questions.q: The acceptable variation around a specific objective is the:
questions.explain: Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around a particular objective; appetite is the broader willingness.

questions.q: Exposure remaining after controls are applied is:
questions.explain: Residual risk is what remains after the chosen response and controls.

questions.q: Which is a valid ERM risk response unique to ERM (vs traditional) thinking?
choices: Pursue (take more risk that advances strategy)
questions.explain: ERM adds 'pursue' — deliberately taking more of a risk that supports strategy — to the response set.

questions.q: For MBG's 15 expired certificates of insurance ($512,000.00 exposure), the best response is:
questions.explain: Compliance controls reduce likelihood and valid insurance transfers the risk; acceptance is inappropriate.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the five COSO ERM components?
questions.explain: The components are governance/culture, strategy/objective-setting, performance, review/revision, and information/communication/reporting.

questions.q: A risk register entry should include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explain: A register records owner, ratings, controls, residual rating, and response — not a competitor's confidential data.
